title: Statement on Proposals to Enhance the Transparency and Public Accountability Of the Board's Stress Testing Framework
summary: Fed Governor Michael Barr dissented against a package of changes to the Federal Reserve's supervisory stress test framework, arguing that the proposed disclosure of models and scenarios will make the stress test weaker, less credible, and lead to overly optimistic projections. Barr stated that if the proposed credit, market, and operational risk model changes were applied to 2024-2025 stress tests, they would have resulted in projected capital ratios approximately 100 basis points higher than under existing models, equivalent to roughly $115 billion of additional capital more optimistically projected.
key_points: Governor Barr dissented against proposed stress test framework changes, citing concerns they would make stress tests weaker and less credible
The proposed changes include disclosure of stress test models and scenarios to the public
If new credit, market, and operational risk models were used for 2024 or 2025 stress tests, projected capital ratios would have been approximately 100 basis points higher than existing models
The more optimistic projections from proposed models represent roughly $115 billion of additional capital
Barr warned banks would likely reduce management buffers and invest less in independent risk management under the new framework
Barr expressed concern that model disclosure would enable banks to shift to riskier assets where models underestimate risks
why_it_matters: This dissent statement reveals significant internal disagreement at the Fed about stress testing transparency. Barr's analysis suggests the proposed changes could result in lower bank capital requirements by approximately 100 bps and $115 billion, potentially weakening the financial system's resilience buffer. Market participants should note that Governor Barr serves as Vice Chair for Supervision, making his dissent on stress test framework changes particularly notable.
market_structure_context: The statement directly addresses stress testing framework changes affecting bank capital requirements and financial system resilience. Key market structure concerns raised include: (1) potential for banks to reduce management buffers above required capital; (2) risk of 'model monoculture' as banks focus on Fed's disclosed models; (3) potential for asset concentration in assets where models give favorable treatment; (4) elimination of regional variation in mortgage loss projections; (5) less conservative probability of default assumptions for corporate loans; (6) weakened loss given default and line of credit draw rate assumptions; (7) shortened liquidity horizons for market shock adjustments; (8) operational risk no longer being macro-sensitive. The 2026 scenario is noted as being at the low end of stressfulness compared to prior tests.
important_numbers: 100 basis points higher projected capital ratios under proposed models
$115 billion additional capital more optimistically projected
notes: This is a dissent statement by Fed Governor Michael Barr, who serves as Vice Chair for Supervision, against proposed stress test framework changes. The source is highly relevant to market structure as it directly addresses bank capital requirements, stress testing methodology, and financial system resilience.
